clusters.label: Too little working protein: haploinsufficiency and destabilized protein
clusters.rationale: In these disorders the cell ends up with too little usable protein, either because one gene copy is lost (haploinsufficiency) or because the variant protein is unstable, degraded or stuck in the endoplasmic reticulum. The therapeutic logic is the same for both routes: raise the amount of working protein, by gene supplementation or by helping the protein fold. This is the cluster that links STXBP1 to SLC6A1 across two unrelated pathways.

clusters.label: Dominant-negative block of vesicle fusion
clusters.rationale: Here the altered protein is still present and jams the fusion machine it belongs to, so the result is worse than simply having half the normal amount. This matters therapeutically: adding a healthy gene copy may not be enough if the bad protein keeps interfering, so these variants may need silencing or allele-specific approaches instead. For STXBP1 the dominant-negative reading is contested, and both sides are attached to the edges.

clusters.label: Too much or badly timed release: Ca2+ sensing and clamping defects
clusters.rationale: A separate group of variants does not reduce release but makes it excessive, poorly timed, or un-clamped at rest: vesicles fuse when they should not. Drugs that push more release (aminopyridines) are a poor fit here and could make things worse, which is why several groups argue for classifying these disorders by variant function rather than by gene.

clusters.label: Presynaptic neuromuscular-junction failure (drug-responsive)
clusters.rationale: The same genes that cause brain disease can also cause fatigable muscle weakness when the failing synapse is the neuromuscular junction. That version is partly treatable today with 3,4-diaminopyridine and cholinesterase inhibitors. This is the most actionable cluster in the slice: it means a family with a presynaptic congenital myasthenic syndrome in SYT2, SNAP25 or UNC13A should be assessed for an existing drug, not only for future gene therapy.

clusters.label: SNAREopathies: one presynaptic fusion machine, many diagnoses
clusters.rationale: Every gene here encodes a part of the machine that fuses a synaptic vesicle with the nerve-cell membrane, or a protein that regulates it. Patients receive very different diagnoses (epileptic encephalopathy, febrile-seizure epilepsy, a movement disorder, a myasthenic syndrome), but reviews argue these are one disease family, so research assets and trial designs may be shareable.

clusters.label: Ion-channel, receptor and signalling DEEs
clusters.rationale: Ten genes whose disorders are developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (ILAE 2022, PMID:35503712) and which a 2025 review groups by pathophysiologic category (channelopathies, receptor dysfunction, synaptic signalling; PMID:40381457). Quotes: PMID:40381457: "This comprehensive review explores the evolving landscape of precision therapeutics for DEEs, focusing on mechanism-driven interventions across key pathophysiologic categories." | PMID:40381457: "Targeted approaches for channelopathies include antisense oligonucleotides and gene therapies, such as zorevunersen and ETX101 for SCN1A-related Dravet syndrome, alongside novel small molecules for other ion channel disorders." | PMID:40381457: "For synaptic dysfunctions, innovative treatments such as chemical chaperones for STXBP1-related disorders and Ras-Raf-MEK-ERK inhibitors for SYNGAP1 pathologies are discussed." | PMID:35503712: "The emerging class of etiology-specific epilepsy syndromes, where there is a specific etiology for the epilepsy that is associated with a clearly defined, relatively uniform, and distinct clinical phenotype in most affected individuals as well as consistent EEG, neuroimaging, and/or genetic correlates, is presented."

clusters.label: Sodium-channel gain of function: sodium channel blockers reported to help
clusters.rationale: Gain-of-function SCN2A, SCN8A and (rare) SCN1A variants; the sources report response to sodium channel blockers (PMID:28379373, 34431999, 35696452).

clusters.label: Sodium-channel loss of function: sodium channel blockers reported to worsen
clusters.rationale: Loss-of-function SCN1A (Dravet), later-onset SCN2A and SCN8A LoF; sources describe sodium channel blockers as worsening or contraindicated (PMID:9596203, 36314457, 28379373, 41515912). Recorded as counter-evidence.

clusters.label: Same gene, opposite mechanisms
clusters.rationale: Genes where both gain- and loss-of-function variants cause disease; trial eligibility criteria already split by mechanism (NCT06872125, NCT04639310, NCT05818553, NCT07019922).

clusters.label: Shared symptoms with the SNAREopathies, different mechanisms
clusters.rationale: HPO profiles of these DEE and SNAREopathy disorders are in the top 1% of similarity for both diseases, while their molecular mechanisms differ (ion channels/receptors/signalling vs presynaptic vesicle fusion).

clusters.label: Lysosomal storage disorders: one organelle, many enzymes
clusters.rationale: All twelve genes encode lysosomal proteins: ten digestive enzymes and two membrane proteins (NPC1, CLN3). Whatever the gene, the end result is the same: undigested material piles up in the lysosome (PMID:30275469). The diagnoses look very different (an enlarged spleen in Gaucher disease, kidney and heart disease in Fabry disease, muscle weakness in Pompe disease, childhood dementia in CLN2 disease) but the treatment logic is shared: replace the enzyme, reduce the substrate, or help a misfolded enzyme fold. Within the family, sub-pathways (sphingolipid, glycosaminoglycan, glycogen, cholesterol) group the diseases further.

clusters.label: Chaperone-responsive misfolded proteins (lysosomal and beyond)
clusters.rationale: In these disorders many missense variants still make a protein that could work, but it misfolds and is held back or destroyed in the endoplasmic reticulum. A small molecule that stabilizes the protein can let part of it through: migalastat is approved for amenable GLA variants, ambroxol (GBA1) and pyrimethamine (HEXA) have reached patients, arimoclomol is approved for NPC though its label says its mechanism is unknown, and a chaperone stabilized mutant GAA in mice. The same logic, with a different drug (4-phenylbutyrate), is being tested in two SNAREopathy-layer disorders, SLC6A1 and STXBP1. The shared limit: only variants that fold 'nearly right' respond (the migalastat amenability assay), so the variant, not the gene, decides who can benefit.

clusters.label: Neurological forms where intravenous enzyme replacement can't cross the blood-brain barrier
clusters.rationale: Infused enzymes are large proteins that do not cross the blood-brain barrier (PMID:33304924), so the approved intravenous enzymes treat the body but not the brain: the current Cerezyme label is limited to non-CNS manifestations of type 1 or 3 Gaucher disease, the Xenpozyme label to non-CNS manifestations of ASMD, and laronidase does not cross into the brain in Hurler syndrome. The diseases that are mainly neurological are treated only by approaches that get around the barrier: enzyme infused into the brain ventricles (cerliponase alfa, CLN2), gene-corrected blood stem cells (atidarsagene autotemcel, MLD), early stem-cell transplantation (Krabbe), an enzyme fused to a transferrin-receptor antibody (pabinafusp alfa, MPS II), spinal-fluid AAV (Tay-Sachs), or small molecules that cross the barrier (miglustat, ambroxol). Tay-Sachs, CLN3 and Krabbe disease still have no approved disease-modifying therapy.

clusters.label: RASopathies: one signalling pathway turned up
clusters.rationale: Twelve genes, many diagnoses (Noonan syndrome, NSML, Costello, cardiofaciocutaneous syndrome, neurofibromatosis type 1, Mazzanti syndrome, CBL syndrome), one pathway: each gene encodes a component or regulator of RAS/MAPK signalling and the vast majority of disease variants increase signalling (PMID:19467855, PMID:23875798, PMID:29924299, PMID:38929714); ClinGen curated the gene set (PMID:30311384). Shared pathway means shared drug targets: MEK inhibitors approved for NF1 are being repurposed across the family.

clusters.label: MEK-inhibitor-responsive RAS/MAPK overactivation
clusters.rationale: Diseases where blocking MEK has been approved (NF1 plexiform neurofibromas: selumetinib, mirdametinib), used off-label with reported benefit (RAF1 and RIT1 hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, SOS1 lymphatic disease) or is being trialled (MEKinRAS phase 2; Baby MERIT phase 3, which admits Noonan/Costello/CFC genes including recessive LZTR1 but excludes NSML-type PTPN11). CFC MEK1 variants are MEK-inhibitor-sensitive in vitro (PMID:17981815) but no clinical report was found. Limits: case-level evidence, one withdrawn 2012 trial, and no completed randomised trial outside NF1.

clusters.label: Loss of RAS regulation (NF1, LZTR1, CBL)
clusters.rationale: Most RASopathy genes are activated accelerators; these three are lost brakes. Neurofibromin is a RAS GTPase-activating protein (PMID:35066574), LZTR1 tags RAS for ubiquitination and removal from the membrane (PMID:30442762, PMID:30442766) and CBL ubiquitylates receptors (PMID:20619386). Loss-of-function variants (truncating, splice, deletions) dominate their ClinVar spectra, and tumour predisposition via a second hit is shared (NF1 neurofibromas, LZTR1 schwannomas, CBL JMML).

clusters.label: Same gene, different mechanism (PTPN11, LZTR1, RAF1)
clusters.rationale: PTPN11 Noonan variants activate SHP2 (PMID:11704759) whereas NSML variants are catalytically defective and dominant negative (PMID:16377799) and truncating variants cause metachondromatosis (PMID:21533187). Therapy follows mechanism: NSML-type PTPN11 is excluded from the infant MEK-inhibitor trial (NCT07817186) and responded to mTOR inhibition in mice (PMID:21339643), with human-tissue caution (PMID:31722741). LZTR1 dominant variants hit substrate recognition while recessive and schwannomatosis alleles are loss of function (PMID:30481304, PMID:39140257). RAF1 HCM-hotspot variants are kinase-activating while others are kinase impaired (PMID:17603483).

gaps.about: STX1A as a Mendelian disease gene
gaps.question: Is STX1A an established Mendelian disease gene, and under which entity?
what_is_missing: No OMIM gene-phenotype entry: Monarch returns no OMIM causal edge for STX1A.
Orphanet links STX1A only as 'Role in the phenotype of' Williams syndrome (a contiguous-gene deletion) and 'Modifying germline mutation in' cystic fibrosis.
Gene2Phenotype confidence is moderate for a neurodevelopmental disorder with epilepsy and limited without epilepsy; ClinGen has no classification.
No HPO annotations exist for any STX1A-specific entity, so it has no phenotype profile and cannot enter the phenotype-similarity comparison.
searched: Orphadata rd-associated-genes for ORPHA:904 and ORPHA:586
Open Targets gene2phenotype / clingen / orphanet / genomics_england evidence
gaps.how_to_find_out: One peer-reviewed case series (PMID:36564538, eight individuals) exists and calls this a SNAREopathy. A ClinGen gene-curation expert panel classification, or a second independent cohort with functional data, would settle it. We keep STX1A in the graph with gene_disease_validity recorded as G2P moderate / ClinGen absent.

gaps.question: What is the molecular mechanism of CPLX1-related disease in human neurons?
what_is_missing: No functional study of patient CPLX1 variants in neurons was found.
The mechanism rests on the discovery paper's own cautious wording about loss of complexin-1 function.
ClinGen and Gene2Phenotype have no classification for CPLX1.
searched: PubMed via MCP (CPLX1 complexin-1 variant/function/neuron queries)
gaps.how_to_find_out: Patient-derived or knock-in neurons measuring spontaneous versus evoked release would show whether CPLX1 variants de-clamp spontaneous release (as complexin's clamping role predicts) or reduce evoked release.

gaps.question: Do NSF variants act by a dominant-negative effect in neurons?
what_is_missing: The dominant-negative claim comes from a Drosophila eye-development assay, not neurons.
No electrophysiology in mammalian neurons or patient-derived cells was found.
Only one Mendelian NSF report exists (PMID:31675180).
searched: PubMed via MCP (NSF epileptic encephalopathy / function queries)
Open Targets (only Genomics England amber for DEE96)
gaps.how_to_find_out: Express the patient variants in Nsf-null or wild-type mammalian neurons and measure SNARE-complex turnover and release. NSF is a recycling ATPase, so a dominant-negative effect is plausible but unproven.

gaps.question: Does 4-phenylbutyrate help patients, and does it correct the mutant protein or boost the healthy copy?
what_is_missing: No completed trial with posted efficacy results: NCT04937062 (STXBP1 + SLC6A1) is early phase 1 and its primary endpoints are safety and tolerability; NCT07847918 tests the feasibility of a remote trial design.
The only human outcome data found is two uncontrolled patients with 3p deletions (PMID:39923323), who have no misfolded protein to correct.
Whether the drug acts on the mutant or on wild-type trafficking is unresolved by the proponents' own statement (PMID:35911425).
No study stratifies response by variant class (ER-retained versus surface-expressed), which is the prediction that would test the mechanism.
searched: PubMed via MCP (phenylbutyrate / chaperone + STXBP1 / SLC6A1)
ClinicalTrials.gov API v2 (NCT04937062, NCT07847918, NCT07173153, NCT06983158)
gaps.how_to_find_out: A trial or n-of-1 series that reports outcomes separately for ER-retained versus surface-expressed variants. The functional classifications already exist (PMID:34028503, PMID:38781976), so existing cohorts could be re-analysed by variant class.

gaps.question: Can each pathogenic variant be assigned to a mechanism class, rather than each gene?
what_is_missing: Our variant_group nodes are consequence classes from ClinVar, not functional classes.
Published functional data covers only tens of variants per gene, against 495 P/LP ClinVar records for STXBP1 and 243 for SLC6A1.

Several genes show opposite effects for different variants (SNAP25 I67N versus V48F; STX1B G226R versus V216E; UNC13A dominant versus recessive), so gene-level mechanism labels are unsafe for choosing a therapy.
gaps.how_to_find_out: Link each ClinVar VCV to published functional readouts (surface expression, protein level, evoked and spontaneous release) in a variant-level table. The field is explicitly calling for this (PMID:41166419).

gaps.question: Why does one SNAP25 variant cause a myasthenic syndrome while others cause epileptic encephalopathy?
what_is_missing: OMIM 616330 is 'congenital myasthenic syndrome 18', but ClinGen classifies SNAP25 as Definitive for genetic developmental and epileptic encephalopathy. The umbrella covers both, and HPO annotations exist only for the myasthenic entity.
No study compares neuromuscular-junction and central phenotypes for the same variant set.
searched: Monarch v3 entities for MONDO:0014590 and MONDO:0700466
Open Targets ClinGen and Genomics England evidence
gaps.how_to_find_out: A cohort reporting neuromuscular testing (repetitive nerve stimulation) in SNAP25-DEE patients would show whether subclinical neuromuscular involvement is common and therefore drug-addressable.

gaps.question: Why do Tay-Sachs (HEXA), CLN3 disease and Krabbe disease (GALC) still have no approved disease-modifying therapy, while nine of the twelve family members do?
what_is_missing: No FDA label was found for any HEXA, CLN3 or GALC product (openFDA searched by brand for every approved lysosomal product in this family).
CLN3: an open-label miglustat study states 'No disease-modifying treatments are currently available' (PMID:40924969); n=6, historical controls.
HEXA: only pyrimethamine (phase I/II, dose-limited by side effects; PMID:20926324, PMID:21185210) and a two-patient intrathecal AAV expanded-access report (PMID:35145305).
GALC: haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is the only disease-modifying option and works only when done early (PMID:27638597).
searched: openFDA drug label API (brand names for 19 approved lysosomal products)
PubMed: pyrimethamine[ti] AND (Tay-Sachs OR GM2 OR hexosaminidase)
PubMed: (Tay-Sachs[ti] OR GM2[ti]) AND AAV AND gene therapy AND patients
PubMed: Krabbe[ti] AND (cord blood OR transplantation) AND infantile
ClinicalTrials.gov API v2 query.cond: Tay-Sachs Disease, GM2 Gangliosidosis, CLN3 Disease, Juvenile Neuronal Ceroid Lipofuscinosis, Krabbe Disease, Globoid Cell Leukodystrophy
gaps.how_to_find_out: All three are dominated by brain disease, which intravenous enzymes cannot reach (cluster:lysosomal-bbb-barrier). Track the registered CNS-directed gene-therapy and small-molecule trials linked to these diseases in the atlas; ask the patient organisations (NTSAD, Beyond Batten, Hunter's Hope) about programmes not yet registered.

gaps.question: What treats the brain disease in the neuronopathic forms of diseases whose approved enzymes only treat the body (Gaucher types 2/3, ASMD type A, MPS I Hurler, neuronopathic MPS II)?
what_is_missing: The current Cerezyme label covers only non-CNS manifestations of type 1 or type 3 Gaucher disease; the Xenpozyme label only non-CNS manifestations of ASMD.
Laronidase does not cross the blood-brain barrier (PMID:15895714).

The brain-penetrant options found are clinical-stage only: ambroxol for neuronopathic Gaucher (systematic review, PMID:39116528) and pabinafusp alfa for MPS II (phase 2/3, PMID:33038326). Any regulatory approval of pabinafusp alfa was not verified from a fetched label, so it is recorded as stage 'clinical'.
searched: openFDA labels: CEREZYME, VPRIV, ELELYSO, XENPOZYME, ELAPRASE (ALDURAZYME returned no openFDA label)
PubMed: laronidase AND ("blood-brain barrier" OR "central nervous system") AND (Hurler OR "MPS I")
PubMed: ambroxol[ti] AND Gaucher AND chaperone
PubMed: "enzyme replacement therapy" AND "blood-brain barrier" AND "lysosomal storage" AND review[pt]
gaps.how_to_find_out: Follow the CNS-directed studies linked to these diseases (e.g. NCT04573023 and NCT05371613 for MPS II); check PMDA (Japan) and EMA records for pabinafusp alfa, which the atlas could not fetch as a label.

gaps.question: Which variants in GBA1, HEXA, NPC1 and GAA are 'amenable' to a chaperone, the way GLA variants are classified for migalastat?
what_is_missing: Only GLA has a regulator-accepted variant-level amenability test (the GALAFOLD label restricts use to an amenable GLA variant 'based on in vitro assay data').

For GBA1 (ambroxol), HEXA (pyrimethamine) and NPC1 (arimoclomol) the evidence is per drug, not per variant; for ambroxol the chaperone action itself is questioned for some variants (PMID:38797393), and the arimoclomol label says its mechanism in NPC is unknown.
Our variant_group nodes are ClinVar consequence classes (e.g. 574 GLA missense P/LP records), not functional amenability classes.
searched: PubMed queries listed under the migalastat, ambroxol, pyrimethamine, NPC1 I1061T and GAA chaperone claims (pipeline/families/lysosomal/curation.py)
gaps.how_to_find_out: A cross-gene, variant-level table of misfolding readouts (ER retention, stability, response to chaperone in patient cells), like the one regulators accepted for migalastat. The same table would also test the cross-family bridge to SLC6A1, where about a third of loss-of-function missense variants reach the surface and are outside a chaperone's reach (PMID:38781976).

gaps.question: What does the CLN3 protein do, and what exactly is stored?
what_is_missing: CLN3 is a lysosomal membrane protein, not an enzyme; we found no curated statement of its molecular function, so disease:CLN3 has no enzyme-deficiency or loss-of-function mechanism edge, only lysosomal storage (PMID:27491213).
GO annotations for CLN3 are mostly inferred (IEA/ISS), apart from lysosomal lumen acidification and lysosomal transport (IMP).
searched: PubMed: CLN3[ti] AND (Batten OR "neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis") AND lysosom* AND review[pt]
QuickGO annotations for UniProtKB:Q13286 (16 candidate processes)
gaps.how_to_find_out: Recent structural and lipidomic studies of CLN3 (not yet curated here) should be reviewed by a biochemist before a mechanism edge is added.

gaps.question: Do lysosomal and SNAREopathy disorders overlap in symptoms enough to be confused clinically?
what_is_missing: With the same method and thresholds as the SNAREopathy layer (Resnik BMA, >= 95th percentile for both diseases and >= 99th for one), no cross-family pair qualified.

Near misses in the top 5% of both backgrounds: GALC-UNC13A (97.1/97.4%), GBA1-UNC13A (96.9/97.3%), TPP1-STXBP1 (96.5/95.7%), ARSA-STXBP1 (96.7/95.3%), GAA-SYT2 (96.0/95.8%: two causes of neuromuscular weakness). They are recorded in data/raw/families/lysosomal/hpo_stats.json, not drawn as edges.
searched: phenotype.hpoa 2026-09-02 / hp.obo 2026-09-01; SNAREopathy profiles from data/raw/biology/hpo_stats.json
gaps.how_to_find_out: A clinician review of the near-miss pairs (e.g. whether CLN2 disease enters the differential of early-onset epileptic encephalopathy alongside STXBP1, which would argue for including TPP1 in epilepsy gene panels).

gaps.question: How should GBA1's role in Parkinson disease be represented?
what_is_missing: Monarch records GBA1 -> late-onset Parkinson disease and Lewy body dementia as 'contributes_to' (OMIM), and Orphanet as 'Major susceptibility factor in' (ORPHA:411602). These are susceptibility links, so they are excluded from the GBA1 umbrella's subtypes and causes edge (listed in attrs.excluded_susceptibility_links).
searched: Monarch v3 CausalGeneToDiseaseAssociation and CorrelatedGeneToDiseaseAssociation for HGNC:4177
gaps.how_to_find_out: If the atlas adds a Parkinson disease family, link it to gene:GBA1 with a susceptibility relation rather than 'causes'; the ambroxol chaperone work spans both (PMID:38797393).

gaps.question: Which lysosomal communities lack a verified patient organisation, registry or research group in the atlas?
what_is_missing: CLN2 (TPP1): only one verified organisation (Noah's Hope); CLN3 organisations other than Beyond Batten name only the umbrella 'Batten disease'.
No registry page was verified for Gaucher, Fabry, Tay-Sachs, MPS II or MLD (registry studies found on ClinicalTrials.gov are included as assets instead).

No research group met the threshold (>= 2 senior-author papers among the 80 most recent title-matched papers) for Gaucher, MPS I or MPS II: the literature is spread over many groups. NIH RePORTER was not searched for this family.
ARSA: No MLD registry or natural-history study described on stored pages.
CLN3: No CLN3-specific registry found; Batten-wide BDCRC network and natural-history study recorded from the URBC page (umbrella term 'Batten disease').
GAA: No Pompe registry description was stored: IPA ('Pompe Registry') and AMDA ('Patient Registry') mention one only as menu links; the MDA Pompe page returned HTTP 404.

GALC: No Krabbe registry described explicitly; KrabbeCURES recorded as a research-participation platform. Partners for Krabbe Research (p4kr.org) and Legacy of Angels (legacyofangels.org) did not resolve (DNS).
GBA1: No Gaucher registry or natural-history study is described on the stored pages (Gauchers Association lists research projects such as Rapsodi and Gaucherite only as menu links).
GLA: No Fabry registry or natural-history study described on stored pages; National Fabry Disease Foundation (fabrydisease.org) fetch failed (HTTP 307 redirect loop).
HEXA: No GM2/Tay-Sachs registry description stored (CATS Foundation lists a 'Registry' only as a menu link).
IDS: No MPS II-specific registry or natural-history study described on stored pages; MPS Society Australia fetch failed (connection refused).
searched: Organisation websites listed in pipeline/families/lysosomal/web_sources.json (stored under data/raw/families/lysosomal/web/)
ClinicalTrials.gov API v2 condition searches (titles with Registry / Natural History / Outcome Survey)
gaps.how_to_find_out: Search NIH RePORTER per disease (pipeline/community/fetch_reporter.py shows how), widen the PubMed window for Gaucher and MPS, and ask the umbrella groups (BDSRA, National MPS Society, NTSAD) for registries they run.

gaps.question: Does MEK inhibition improve outcomes in Noonan-spectrum hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or lymphatic disease, beyond case reports?
what_is_missing: No completed randomised or controlled trial outside NF1: MEKinRAS (NCT06555237, phase 2) is recruiting and Baby MERIT (NCT07817186, phase 3) is not yet recruiting.
The first MEK-inhibitor trial in Noonan HCM (binimetinib/MEK162, NCT01556568) was withdrawn 'due to scientific and business considerations' with 0 enrolled.
Clinical evidence is case reports/series and one retrospective 61-patient comparison (PMID:40131150) whose abstract does not break results down by gene.
Pulmonary vascular disease did not respond in a RAF1 infant (PMID:35052347).

gaps.question: What treatment fits NSML-type (catalytically impaired) PTPN11 hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
what_is_missing: NSML-causing PTPN11 variants are explicitly excluded from the MEK-inhibitor infant trial (NCT07817186).
mTOR inhibition (rapamycin) is preclinical only (PMID:21339643, PMID:22058153); human NSML heart tissue showed attenuated, not enhanced, mTORC1 activity (PMID:31722741).
Whether NSML mutants behave as loss or gain of function in cardiomyocytes is itself contested (PMID:24935154).
searched: PubMed esearch: LEOPARD[ti] AND Kontaridis MI[au] (5 hits, 2026-10-03)
PubMed esearch: LEOPARD syndrome[tiab] AND SHP2[tiab] AND catalytic activity[tiab] (11 hits, 2026-10-03)
PubMed esearch: rapamycin[tiab] AND LEOPARD[tiab] AND cardiomyopathy[tiab] (6 hits, 2026-10-03)
gaps.how_to_find_out: Patient-derived cardiomyocyte studies comparing MEK and mTOR inhibition in NSML versus Noonan PTPN11 genotypes; a registry arm for NSML-HCM outcomes.

gaps.question: Is MEK inhibition used or tested in cardiofaciocutaneous (BRAF, MAP2K1, KRAS) or Costello (HRAS) syndrome?
what_is_missing: CFC MEK1 variants are sensitive to a tool MEK inhibitor in vitro (PMID:17981815), but our searches found no clinical report or trial specific to CFC or Costello syndrome.
Baby MERIT (NCT07817186) admits Noonan, Costello or CFC genes, so the first prospective data may come from it.

gaps.question: Is there any pathway-targeted treatment for learning and attention problems in NF1 or other RASopathies?
what_is_missing: Statins rescued Nf1+/- mice (PMID:16271875) but failed in two randomised trials in children (PMID:18632543, PMID:27956565).
A lovastatin/lamotrigine RASopathy trial (NCT03504501) terminated for recruitment difficulties.
No MEK-inhibitor cognition trial was found in our ClinicalTrials.gov searches.

gaps.how_to_find_out: Check the NF Clinical Trials Consortium and CTF pipeline for neurocognitive endpoints in ongoing MEK-inhibitor trials.

gaps.question: Which individual variants are activating, catalytically impaired or loss of function?
what_is_missing: Variant groups are ClinVar consequence classes; PTPN11 missense variants include both activating (Noonan) and catalytically impaired (NSML) alleles, and RAF1 includes kinase-activating and kinase-impaired alleles (PMID:17603483).
LZTR1 has dominant (Kelch-surface) and recessive/loss-of-function classes (PMID:30481304).
Multi-gene CNVs dominate SHOC2, CBL, HRAS and LZTR1 (22q11.2) ClinVar records and get no mechanism edge.

gaps.question: Is any interventional study open to SHOC2-, CBL- or HRAS-related disorders specifically?
what_is_missing: ClinicalTrials.gov term searches returned 1 SHOC2 record and no SHOC2-, CBL- or Costello-specific interventional trial; CBL appears mainly in leukaemia (JMML) trials, which are out of scope here.
These genes are covered only by multi-gene observational cohorts (NCT04888936; NCT04395495).
gaps.how_to_find_out: Ask the NCI RASopathy cohort (NCT04888936) and RASopathies Network which patients are trial-eligible in the MEK-inhibitor HCM trials.
